sections.overview: The little sparrowhawk is one of Africa’s smallest hawks, a resident of wooded habitats from eastern to southern Africa. It hunts swiftly through trees for small birds and other small vertebrates. The species has also been placed in the genus Tachyspiza in some recent checklists; this profile keeps the project’s scientific name, Accipiter minullus.
sections.identification: This compact hawk has a grey to blackish head and upperparts, finely barred pale underparts, yellow legs and cere, and a long, dark-barred tail. Adults have yellow eyes, which may become more orange-red in the breeding season; juveniles are browner above and spotted rather than barred below. It is about 23–27 cm long, with a wingspan around 39–52 cm. Published mass ranges are approximately 74–85 g for males and 68–105 g for females; the overlap and sparse sampling mean these figures are not a reliable field sexing rule. No useful body height or width measurement was found. Two conspicuous white spots near the base of the upper tail can help identify a perched or flying bird; distinguish it from the larger African goshawk and from the similar Shikra by size, eye colour and detailed plumage.
sections.habitat: It favors patches of dense woodland, forest edges, riverine forest and wooded valleys, as well as stands of trees within savanna and some suburban areas. The species occurs from Ethiopia and parts of eastern Africa south through central and southern Africa to South Africa. It is generally resident, though local movements may occur. It avoids extensive, unbroken rainforest where its hunting style and prey access are less suited.
sections.diet: Small birds are the main prey, caught in a sudden low, fast flight from cover. It also takes small lizards and other vertebrates; regional accounts report frogs, small mammals and insects. The exact diet varies with what is available, and broad prey lists should not be mistaken for equal proportions.
sections.behavior: It is usually encountered alone or in pairs and hunts from a perch or by darting through foliage. Its compact body and long tail help it maneuver between branches. A breeding female can defend the nest vigorously against approaching birds. The species is secretive and may be overlooked even where it is present.
sections.reproduction: The pair nests in trees, and the female incubates while the male supplies food and helps defend the nest. Clutch size and breeding dates vary geographically; southern African sources report one to three eggs, but this should not be generalized to the whole range. Direct information on incubation and fledging is uneven among regions.
sections.ecology: As an agile small-bird predator, it is part of the woodland food web and can also take reptiles, mammals and insects. It uses natural woodland as well as tree patches in more open landscapes, including some planted forests. A regional account suggests it may benefit locally from exotic tree plantations, but this does not establish a continent-wide population increase.
sections.conservation: The species is classified as Least Concern in the references reviewed and has a broad sub-Saharan range. This regional assessment does not rule out local declines where woodland is cleared or fragmented. Current population trends and exact abundance are not well quantified across all countries in its range.
